advocacyHeadline: Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone. These arteries should be safer and more accessible so more people can walk, bike, and get around our city. Pick a perspective below, customize your message, and tell City Council.
defaultSubject: Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone

statements.title: Kids Deserve Independence — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing as a parent who believes kids deserve independence.

Not every high school student can drive, and not every parent can provide transportation. Safe bike infrastructure gives teenagers independence to get to school, visit friends, attend activities, and explore their community. Parents shouldn't have to choose between their children's safety and independence.

At Arroyo Vista, we've seen enormous enthusiasm for biking through our bike bus. But kids need safe routes beyond organized group rides. We should build for the future generation: just because students cannot vote doesn't mean they shouldn't have a stake in transportation decisions. In fact, they will be the ones using the streets in the future.

We tell our kids to be independent, but then we build streets where they need an adult to drive them everywhere. Improving Huntington and Fremont for walking and biking is how we change that.

statements.title: Public Streets Serve Everyone — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing as a resident who believes public streets should serve everyone.

Fremont is already a public roadway, used by people walking, biking, and driving. Under California law, bicyclists generally have the same rights and responsibilities as drivers on public roads. Some homeowners may own the land beneath portions of public sidewalks or streets, but public easements can give the city rights to use and improve that land. The exact boundaries and legal rights need to be clarified — but that should not stop us from making our streets safer for people who already use them.

Fremont is already a public street. We're not asking to introduce a new use, we're asking to make it safer for people who already have the right to use it. The same principle applies to Huntington: these are public arteries that should work for everyone.

statements.title: The Missing Link — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing about Fremont as a missing link in our regional transportation network.

Fremont isn't just a neighborhood bike lane. It's a critical connection between South Pasadena, Pasadena, and Los Angeles. Protected infrastructure becomes significantly more useful when it connects to other safe routes. Without Fremont, important gaps remain in the regional walking and biking network. Our city boundaries shouldn't determine where people can travel safely.

Safe streets shouldn't end at city limits. Fremont is a missing link in a much bigger transportation network — and improving Huntington and Fremont together strengthens that network for everyone who lives here or travels through.

statements.title: Years of Planning Deserve Results — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing as a taxpayer who believes years of planning deserve results.

This project has already gone through extensive community engagement, engineering, and public review. City Council approved moving the preferred design forward. Public resources have already been invested in developing the project. The community deserves to understand what changed, what alternatives are being considered, and how funding will be protected. An indefinite delay shouldn't replace a transparent decision-making process.

At what point does community engagement lead to action? We've had the meetings, heard the feedback, and made a decision. Now we need to find a path forward — for Fremont, for Huntington, and for streets that work for everyone.

statements.title: Safer Streets Benefit Everyone — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing as a driver who believes safer streets benefit everyone.

South Pasadena experiences cut-through traffic from drivers traveling between surrounding communities — 100,000 cars go through South Pas every day with only 30,000 residents. Street safety improvements can benefit people driving, walking, and biking by making movement more predictable. Safety for our most vulnerable will create safety for drivers too.

South Pasadena is passionate about protecting its historic identity. But slowing our streets would maintain residential streets, making it harder for South Pas to be a cut-through city.

Do we want South Pasadena to be a shortcut for commuters, or a community where residents can safely get around? Redesigning Huntington and Fremont for safety and access helps us choose the latter.

statements.title: Build It So People Can Use It — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing as someone who wants to bike more — if our streets make it possible.

One recurring criticism of bike lanes is that not enough people currently bike on certain streets. But current ridership doesn't capture people who would like to bike and don't feel comfortable doing so. In particular, protected infrastructure closes the gender gap in cycling as female cyclists feel safer riding. A protected network makes biking more accessible to children, older adults, and less confident riders. The success of our local bike buses demonstrates an existing interest in family cycling.

We can't use the lack of cyclists on an unsafe street as evidence that we shouldn't make it safer. Why would they want to ride when these streets put their lives at risk? Build safer Huntington and Fremont corridors so people can use them.

statements.title: More Housing Needs More Transportation Options — Huntington and Fremont are for Everyone
statements.body:
Dear Councilmembers,

I am writing because more housing needs more transportation options.

South Pasadena is planning for more housing and population growth, but more residents shouldn't automatically mean more cars on already congested streets. We need to invest in walking, biking, and transit infrastructure alongside new housing. Safe, connected bike networks give residents real alternatives to driving for everyday trips.

Fremont is an opportunity to prepare our city for growth while preserving the character of our residential neighborhoods — and the same is true for Huntington. If we want a livable South Pasadena as we grow, Huntington and Fremont must work for everyone, not only for cars.
